item.title: New role, building an AI product
item.description:
New role at a private-equity–backed software company. We’re building an AI product.

Tooling has changed since the last post. Day-to-day runs on Claude on the 20x Max plan, which has shifted what’s worth attempting in a single sitting — bigger refactors, more in-flight branches, fewer “I’ll come back to this on a clear afternoon” deferrals.

Weather is warm and sunny. Things are good.

item.title: Using Rust for work
item.description:
Writing Rust for work now. Considering a VS Code extension on the side.

AI-assisted typing is genuinely useful — the pace of writing real code has shifted noticeably.

item.title: The First Law
item.description:
Violent, dark, very graphic — and very well done. The character work is what kept me reading. In the second book everything starts to land. Around 60% through book two it grips hard if it hasn’t already.

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_First_Law

item.title: Decisions are like bananas
item.description:
You don’t want to make a decision when it isn’t ripe — the banana is green:

  • someone is pressuring you
  • you haven’t done the research
  • you haven’t worked out whether you have the resources to commit

→ Say let me get back to you. Put it on your TODO list.

You don’t want to make it when it’s overdue — the banana is brown:

  • you avoided it for too long
  • the research never got done
  • you don’t have the resources, and acquiring them now would take too long

→ Say no.

item.title: Project progress
item.description:
The Rust project is on track. Steady day-by-day progress.

The anyhow crate has been great.

I should write more after-action reports. I usually commit lessons to memory by talking them through with colleagues, but writing them down does work better — at least when I bother to do it.

Otherwise this post would be the same as the last one: a tiny blip and a long stretch of silence.

item.title: The Three-Body Problem
item.description:
The Dark Forest, wallfacers and wallbreakers — great concepts. Worth the time.

Book two is the strongest of the trilogy. Book three felt like it could have lived in a different series — closer in tone to The Wandering Earth by the same author. It was hard to finish, but it’s good SF and asks the right questions.

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Three-Body_Problem_(novel)

item.title: Expeditionary Force
item.description:
Skippy and Joe. The series starts as hard military SF, turns into very-well-done Star Trek, and eventually into its own thing.

There’s a mid-series detour into space opera that I’ll blame on Skippy. Some of the harder military fiction split off into its own series starting with Trouble on Paradise; the strategy and scheming stayed with Joe.

Plenty of pop-culture quips throughout, but the through-line is the same: work the problem in front of you.

item.title: Foundation
item.description:
Asimov runs through I, Robot, Bicentennial Man, and Foundation. I watched the screen adaptations long before tracing them back to the source.

Psycho-history is a fun premise. Worth reading.

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foundation_series

item.title: Infinite
item.description:
Infinite and Infinite 2 are both good. Several of Jeremy Robinson’s other novels (Torment, others) tie in as crossovers from Infinite 3 onward.

If you only read two, read 1 and 2. The rest are fun but lighter on the heavy questions.

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Robinson

item.title: Working on a new idea
item.description:
Most of coding isn’t coding — it’s research, tooling, and figuring out whether someone has already solved the problem. I try not to build a solution if there’s a usable one I can adapt. This time I have to do the heavy lifting.

I picked up Flutter again recently. It’s pleasant. There’s a small Flutter side project I’ll come back to, but it’s not a challenge — more of a warm-up puzzle.

item.title: About
item.description:
Why 887? It’s a prime, three letters, fast to type. No deeper meaning.

This is a personal blog. Opinions are my own.

item.title: Red Rising
item.description:
Read the whole series and recommend it. The original trilogy in particular has some sharp ideas worth sitting with.

item.title: Welcome to my blog
item.description:
Starting a blog in 2023, mostly because the backend is markdown and markdown is good to edit anywhere I have git and an editor.

Some markdown files I keep private as a journal; some end up here as posts.

Setup is Hugo on GitHub Pages. I picked Hugo over Jekyll because Go is more familiar to me and I’ve shipped a few real sites with it.

Build runs from a private source repo, the deploy action pushes the rendered public/ folder to a public <user>.github.io repo. The workflow file lives in this repo if you want to copy the pattern.
